scenes.prose:
Seb came in with the wrong kind of quiet.

Marcus noticed it before he looked up from the bench—before the locker room door finished dragging shut behind him. Brent had already made the place into its usual pre-match ecology: hands buried in a shattered coil of strap and seam tape, making it hold. Mathias stood a little apart from the noise, turning his head when someone said something worth catching. Kip paced the edge of the room like forward momentum had learned to wear boots. Useful work. The kind that kept fear from hardening in the joints.

Seb’s footsteps were late enough to change the room’s shape.

He had his scrim kit on, but not cleanly. One cuff half-fastened. One shoulder plate skewed. He’d run here, or nearly run, and used enough effort getting in that it didn’t reach his face—because the face was the part Marcus trusted least on people trying not to fall apart.

Seb stopped near the bench, took one breath, then another that was smaller.

Brent glanced up. “You missed the first warmup and the part where we pretended this was a normal evening.”

Seb nodded, landing somewhere short of agreement. “I know.”

Mathias’ gaze sharpened. “What happened?”

Seb’s mouth worked once before the words came. “My brother died.”

The room went still in the way systems go when assumptions just broke. Kip stopped pacing. Brent’s hands stilled on the strap in his lap; the fabric seemed to hold its breath too.

Marcus felt the statement hit, past the obvious meaning into the structure underneath it. Not a metaphor. Not a plea. A fact delivered late enough to complicate everything around it. Seb still came. That mattered. It changed the weight of the silence that followed.

Mathias asked first, keeping the question in a safe shape. “Before now?”

Seb gave one quick nod. “This morning.”

No performance. No room for one.

Brent exhaled through his nose—too controlled for sympathy, too flat for anything else. “All right,” he said, and made all right mean only that there was still a job to do. “Then we don’t make him carry extra nonsense.”

Seb looked at him once, brief and unreadable, and reached for the strap Brent had been fixing. His fingers were steady enough to be useful, which was worse than if they’d shaken.

Marcus watched the exchange and felt the room settle around a new center of gravity. The grief was there. So was the decision to keep moving inside it. Nobody said that part out loud because praise made pain smaller.

Kip clapped Seb lightly on the back, then seemed to regret it immediately. “You good to run?”

“No,” Seb said. Then, softer: “But yes.”

“That’s enough,” Mathias said—measured, no judgment, only capacity.

Marcus pulled his gloves on more slowly than he needed to. His own hands were calm, which usually meant the useful part of his mind had taken the lead. Tonight it was trying to do two things at once: hold the work anomaly in one hand and the scrim in the other, and it disliked being interrupted.

The anomaly sat under his ribs like a splinter he couldn’t see.

He’d checked cohort data before anyone else arrived. Checked it again. The pattern was still there: directional drift where it had no business existing. It didn’t feel solved. It felt watched. He’d already traced the edges of the logs where the system insisted nothing had crossed. Whatever was wrong stayed below the threshold of being named—annoying in the professional sense, unsettling in the personal one.

He shoved the thought aside when the arena feed on the wall changed from warmup slate to match overlay.

404 on one side.

Dead Hand on the other.

The matchup pulsed in stark white above the field diagram. Hard lines. Calibrated threat markers. Beyond the glass the crowd made soft anticipatory noise, believing they’d come for a contest.

Dead Hand’s reputation was enough to summarize without help: disciplined, patient, hard to read, dangerous where it counted. Their play didn’t waste motion. They didn’t chase. They took what was offered and made the offering look like a mistake. That was enough.

And then there was the benchmark missing from the feed.

Not missing in the literal sense—missing in the sense everyone in the room understood by absence. The star rogue. The role that had been discussed all week in terms that kept stopping just short of naming the threat too plainly. The sort of opponent whose actual performance mattered more than any label because labels were comfort invented by people not about to be tested by them.

Marcus had studied footage to know the benchmark. Not the person. The decision architecture. How a fight could keep folding inward and still leave room for one more mistake that wasn’t a mistake at all. The rhythm. The baiting. The patient pressure. The danger of assuming the first shape a combatant showed was the one that would matter.

The scrim floor lit.

A legal field. Safety wards active. Standard competitive boundaries. Ordinary assumptions laid down like rules everyone pretended were kinder than reality.

Ordinary felt normal right up until it didn’t.

The announcer’s voice rolled from the ceiling in clipped cheer. Teams. Starting positions. Ward limits. No live blades beyond regulation alloy. No outside interference. Contestants began on the horn.

Seb rolled his shoulder once, settled into stance—practiced enough to look habitual, brittle enough to be effort.

Brent came up beside Marcus long enough to check the seal at his wrist. “You’re thinking too hard.”

“I’m thinking the right amount.”

“That’s what people say right before they do something expensive.”

Marcus looked at him. “That is extremely unfair. I usually wait until after.”

Brent made a short sound that might’ve been laughter in a better mood. Then his expression flattened again. “No hero nonsense. If the field starts behaving like it has an attitude, call it.”

Marcus didn’t look away. “Good advice. Rare to see you give it away.”

Brent snorted. “Don’t get sentimental. You won’t survive it.”

Mathias’ voice came from the other side—calm as packed soil. “Left exit is open, but only for three bodies before it closes the lane. Kip, you take it first if we need rotation. Seb, you anchor center unless they force a collapse. Marcus—”

“I know.”

Mathias glanced at him, not annoyed, just confirming. “You adapt.”

Kip looked over. “He means you’re weird in ways that work.”

“Thank you,” Marcus said.

“No,” Brent corrected, voice dry. “He means it in the useful sense.”

Marcus flexed his fingers. The cool pull of the glove against his knuckles grounded him. Neurochromatic Eyes flickered at the edge of his perception, turning the field into layered probability and emphasis. He didn’t need them fully open yet. He needed enough to read the opening without letting the opening read back.

The horn sounded.

The line of 404 surged forward as one organism breaking into parts. Kip drove first—clean aggression, pressure that made hesitation expensive. Brent stayed half a step behind, not support exactly but positioned to keep the angles honest. Mathias drifted where the lane could close and still leave him room to say it had been anticipated. Seb held center—compact, intent, grief turned into function without being made noble by it.

Marcus slid into the seam between them.

Hidden adaptive variable. The kind people only noticed after the shape changed.

Dead Hand answered with less noise than the crowd expected. Their front line met Kip’s push and gave ground with perfect economy—no panic, no waste. Spacing stayed intact.

Then the field changed.

Not with a flare. Not with an announcement. Pressure redistributed across the floor like the match had taken a breath through teeth.

Marcus caught the first sign of the rogue before anyone else did: a red line at the edge of movement, a fraction too fast to be casual. Not color first—motion first. Decision first. Somebody had already decided where the room would be three beats from now.

He turned with it.

The figure came in low—hooded, masked just enough to spoil easy reading. The stance wasn’t right for a standard rush. It was right for someone expecting the field to lie on her behalf. Marcus had seen that kind of decision-making before in footage, until footage stopped being useful and became memory of a pattern.

One clean thought: *That’s her.*

Not who. Not yet. Just the shape of the problem he’d been expecting to meet under a different mask.

She cut through Seb’s line with a twist that would’ve broken lesser balance and made it look accidental. Seb absorbed the contact and stayed standing. Good—because the field would punish anything else.

“Left!” Mathias called.

Kip changed direction instantly, forcing Dead Hand’s second vector to break or overcommit. Brent followed the opening and made it narrower. Marcus moved into the seam.

The rogue came at him on a line almost too clean. Marcus parried once, twice—then realized she wanted the exchange to look like a mistake so she could steal the third beat. Fine. He liked people who made him earn the pattern.

He hit back harder, not to overwhelm but to test the scaffolding. Her defense answered with the same precision he’d expected from benchmark footage, only sharper in the flesh. No wasted motion. No theatricality. Everything chosen.

A blade flashed.

Marcus rolled his shoulder and took the hit on armor instead of flesh. Impact rang through his ribs.

*Okay. That’s real.*

He changed angle, pulled her through a half-step that forced commitment, then snapped his wrist to catch the edge of her hood. Fabric tore.

Red hair spilled free.

His mind stopped pretending the answer was still abstract.

Serra.

The name landed without ceremony, but it hit like recognition never did when it belonged to a person instead of a pattern. He knew the face because he’d seen it in another world under different light—close enough to make air feel smaller. The memory wasn’t complete enough to be safe and not incomplete enough to dismiss. Her mouth tightened as she recovered, and something in her eyes sharpened as the fight kept going.

Then, a half-beat later, strain pushed his own Aspect transition upward—his biometric frame flashed bare for an instant before the next layer took hold.

Serra’s gaze snapped.

The change in her expression was small enough anyone else might’ve missed it. He didn’t. Her focus shifted from tactical to personal as her body adjusted to him.

That was when the match gained a second weight.

Not romance. Not a neat story people tried to tell later. Just meaning—sudden and specific. The dangerous kind. The kind that made both of them better and worse at the same time.

She struck harder. He met it.

The fight tightened around them. Exchanges sped up, each answer less about surprise and more about refusal: denying the other the easy line, the clean finish, the misstep that became a point. Crowd noise blurred into a distant weather system.

Brent shouted about a flank. Kip answered with a grunt and bodies crashing. Seb’s breathing turned rough but steady—the sound of someone doing their work because the alternative would have been worse.

Marcus thought: *So that’s what this is.*

A real opponent. A benchmark. Also a specific problem he hadn’t known he was already carrying.

Serra moved first.

Marcus met her.

Then the field lights stuttered.

Not the arena. Not the ward. The light around the far edge of the scrim shifted with intrusive precision that didn’t belong in a standard contest. A suited figure stood at the boundary—still, composed, presence tuned to make the air feel like it had been instructed to step aside.

Marcus felt the room notice it before he fully understood what he was seeing.

A calm procedural voice came through the arena speakers—completely out of keeping with the match.

“Cease all nonessential escalation. This contest is now under compliance review.”

Marcus kept his blade up because Serra was still in front of him and because compliance review sounded like a phrase designed to make obedience feel like weather.

The voice continued, as if reading from a form someone else decided mattered more than the people in the field.

“By directive authority, participation will continue under constrained conditions. Refusal will be recorded as noncompliance and treated accordingly.”

Brent barked a laugh without humor. “That’s not a review. That’s a gun with paperwork.”

Mathias went very still. “Exit lanes?”

“Locked,” Kip said, looking toward the edges. His voice flattened. “All of them.”

Seb shifted one foot—still facing Dead Hand, still breathing through whatever his brother’s death had hollowed out of him. “We’re being told to keep going,” he said. The worst part was how calm it sounded.

Marcus looked at the boundary again: the suited figure, the hard geometry of the field pretending it had always been this way.

No better option. Not because there wasn’t a path—because the field had been edited into one.

Brent’s words came flat as counted consent. “We don’t have a better option.”

Mathias didn’t argue. He checked exits, the lock, the field, then returned his attention to the fight. “We continue,” he said, because he’d tracked the missing pieces and found the door already closing.

Kip rolled his shoulders once and gave a short, sharp exhale. “Fine. Then we make it ugly.”

Marcus tightened his grip and kept his eyes on Serra.

She’d returned to stance, hood gone, red hair loose, face open to the match in a way it hadn’t been a moment ago. Recognition in her gaze hadn’t softened the fight. If anything, it sharpened the line between them.

Dead Hand was still the enemy. The scrim was still live. The field still held.

And now the contest had started to mean something it hadn’t meant a minute ago—while the match itself remained exactly what it had been told to be.

Marcus shifted his weight, found her center, and moved in again.

Match started. Ordinary competitive assumptions still framed the fight—while Marcus, grounded in tactical language and adaptive readiness, engaged Dead Hand under the constraints and expectations everyone pretended were normal.

scenes.prose:
Brent had just said, “If it looks like a choice, that’s because somebody already decided for you,” when the first blade came through the dark between the scrim pylons.

Marcus moved before the thought finished arranging itself.

The attacker came in low, not at Brent’s centerline but at the gap under his guard, choosing the narrow opening beneath the angle of his weapon and the turn of his shoulder. It was the kind of entry that forced a defender to either give ground or take steel to the ribs. Not a reckless lunge. Not a flourish. A decision. The kind that didn’t care about the shape of a defense because it had already decided the defense was only a temporary inconvenience.

That was the first thing Marcus saw.

Not the weapon. Not the hood. Not the black wrap that broke up outline against the lit floor. The decision architecture: convert the nearest fixed point into a lever, hit through the response, keep pressure on the thing that could not afford to move.

Brent was that thing. Load-bearing, obvious once seen. He was the anchor because he was the one everyone would protect if they had time to think, and the one everyone would hesitate over if they didn’t. So she wasn’t trying to kill Brent first. She was trying to make him into the shape the rest of them had to orbit. Take him out of the rhythm and the whole exchange would become clumsy.

Marcus slid between them and caught the strike on the edge of his forearm guard. The impact jarred up his elbow hard enough to make his teeth click. He twisted with it, used the contact to turn her blade offline, and the next second her free hand was already moving—not a retreat, a transfer. The missed entry became a hook for a second attack, her weight shifting with the sort of efficiency that made the air itself seem wasteful around her.

The abilities were different. The decision wasn’t.

Dead Hand.

The recognition landed without ceremony, and the unpleasant part was that it didn’t feel like surprise. It felt like finding the last piece of a model where he’d already been certain the model was going to be ugly.

“Brent,” Marcus said, not looking away as the hooded fighter slid around his flank. “Try not to be the obvious one.”

“Helpful,” Brent muttered, backing up a step and bringing his weapon up in a hard, practical line. “You always this encouraging when people are trying to stab us?”

“Only when they’re doing it efficiently.”

She came again. Marcus caught her wrist, felt the compact strength in it, the refusal to waste torque, and knew at once she was testing the seam between him and the rest of the line. Not for the first time. Not randomly. She’d already seen the shape of their coordination and was cutting at the points where it would need time to think.

Kip surged in from Marcus’s left with a shove meant to break her angle. She pivoted off the pressure, used his momentum, and snapped a kick at his knee. He barely checked it in time. The exchange was too fast for clean language. The best Marcus could do was keep reading the pattern while his body tried to survive it.

Professional. Tactical. Annoyingly disciplined.

And underneath that discipline, something that made the whole thing feel slightly wrong in a way he couldn’t yet name. Not emotion. Not yet. But a kind of selection pressure that kept returning to specific edges of the team, specific responses, as if the fight had already been scored and she was just removing the pieces most likely to make the score inconvenient.

Brent again. Not because Brent was weakest—Marcus didn’t think that, and neither did she. Because Brent was the support point. Hit him and the rest of them would spend three beats compensating. Three beats was enough.

Marcus cut across her path and forced her to disengage from Brent, or at least pay for it. She took the payment without complaint, letting his interruption turn into her next angle, and for an instant the three of them folded into a shape that almost made sense. Her pressure, his interference, Brent’s refusal to break.

Then her blade flashed up under Marcus’s guard and opened skin along his ribs.

Heat. Immediate and thin. Not a serious wound yet, but enough to make his breath catch and the whole world narrow.

“Marcus!” Mathias’s voice cut from the rear, calm the way a cliff edge was calm. “She’s closing exits.”

Marcus saw it a heartbeat after the words. Of course she was. Not just cornering. Reclassifying. Every time someone shifted to cover Brent, the gap that opened became her next route. Every response became an offering. She wasn’t just attacking the team; she was converting their coordination into her terrain.

That was the point at which he stopped thinking of her as a dangerous assassin and started thinking of her as a real problem.

Not status. Not reputation. Play.

He feinted high, then drove low, forcing her to rotate. She met him without hesitation, and the first touch of their weapons shivered down the line of his forearm. She was fast, but that wasn’t enough to define her. Fast could be panic. Fast could be instinct. This was faster than that. This was choice refined into muscle.

He pressed her toward a support pillar, then deliberately opened a lane to see whether she would take it. She didn’t. She used the opening to hit Kip instead, glancing his shoulder hard enough to stagger him and immediately turning the stagger into space. That tiny decision—strike the new problem, not the nearest target—confirmed what Marcus had been assembling since the first exchange.

She didn’t fight the board in front of her. She rewrote it.

“Brent,” Mathias said, too measured to be alarmed and therefore more alarming, “move left. She’s using your line.”

“I know what she’s doing,” Brent snapped, and Marcus heard the irritation that covered how close it was. “I’m not the one who’s been made into a prop.”

“That’s not better,” Marcus said, and then had no room left for speech.

She came through an angle he hadn’t expected, caught his wrist, and used the brief lock to rip him forward into her knee. His breath left him in a hard, involuntary burst. He turned the impact into a spin, got one hand on her shoulder, and yanked.

Her hood tore.

For one suspended second the face beneath it was just a face, and then the red hair spilled free in a bright, unmistakable fan across her cheek and jaw, lit harshly by the scrim lights. The sight hit him so hard it felt physical. Not because it was beautiful, though it was. Because it was specific. Because the whole room sharpened around a thing he had known in another context, with another kind of attention, and the knowledge came up through him like a blade finding the same old crack.

Serra.

He saw it at once and hated how much his body understood before his brain caught up.

“Serra,” he said, and the name came out quieter than he meant.

Her eyes changed.

Not soft. Not startled in any ordinary sense. The change was subtler and worse: a recalibration. The instant her face registered him, something in her posture revised itself around a fact she had not had a second ago. The fight stayed violent, but the violence no longer sat at the center of her attention. He had entered it.

Then his Aspect shifted.

Just a light shell-change, a brief surface flicker as he leaned on the next layer of protection and the system threaded an unmodified biometric read through the transition. It was only a beat—barely enough to exist—but her gaze snagged on it. He saw the instant the realization hit her, saw the exact moment the anonymous body and the known absence between them snapped into alignment.

Marcus Vye.

Her breath changed. So did her grip.

That second was enough for her to drive her elbow into his shoulder and spin out of his hold, but not enough to erase what had landed. The fight didn’t stop. It got sharper.

“You,” she said, and there was no warmth in it. Only a hard, flat astonishment that sounded almost more dangerous than anger.

“Apparently,” Marcus said, because the alternative was to acknowledge that the last time he had seen her this close, close had meant something he had no language for in the middle of a duel.

She was already moving again. Red hair half-loosed from the torn hood, blade in hand, body resetting into a line that said she had adjusted to the fact of him without giving him the comfort of thinking that adjustment had made her slower. If anything, she was better now. Not because of sentiment. Because the target had become legible.

That was the part he could trust.

Recognition didn’t make her hesitate. It made her dangerous in a cleaner way.

She came at him with a feint low and a slash high, then switched the rhythm mid-motion when he answered too quickly. Marcus barely got his guard up. She clipped his shoulder, drove him into the support pillar he’d been trying to use, and he felt the impact ring through the stone and into his back. Pain flared bright along his ribs. Somewhere to his right, Kip cursed and stumbled, and Brent was still in it, still trying to hold the line without becoming the line.

Marcus shifted into a tighter aspect and the next exchange came in fragments: her wrist rolling under his parry, his knee checking her hip, the edge of her boot catching his shin hard enough to threaten the joint. Not graceful. Not a match to be admired from a distance. A live collision of two people who had just become too interesting to each other to afford mistakes.

That thought was absurd enough to annoy him.

She ducked under his swing, and he caught the back of her hood in his left hand and yanked. The fabric gave, then tore free entirely. Red hair flashed again, brighter now, and her face was fully exposed. The line of her mouth tightened when she saw his expression, as if she had been waiting to know exactly what it cost him to know.

He didn’t give her the satisfaction.

“Of course it’s you,” he said, and immediately regretted how much that sounded like a confession of pattern rather than surprise.

Her answer was to drive a short blade toward his throat.

He caught it on the collar guard, shoved hard, and the two of them separated just enough for the room to rush back in.

Brent was breathing hard on Marcus’s left. Mathias had moved to seal a gap near the exit, eyes tracking every angle with that maddeningly patient precision. Seb was late—still late, because his brother was dead and grief had pinned him half a beat behind reality since they entered the room. Marcus saw the delay in the way Seb reset his stance, saw the effort of it. There was no time to drag him into the fight more gently. The fight didn’t allow gentleness.

Serra saw it too. Of course she did.

Her gaze flicked once toward Brent, once toward Mathias, and the pattern in her body changed again. She had identified the load-bearing point already. Now she was identifying the rest of the structure. It was almost insulting how fast she read them. Almost.

Then she attacked.

Not Brent this time. Him.

The choice changed the whole geometry. Her pressure hit Marcus directly, with no intermediary, and the force of it told him something ugly and satisfying: she’d decided he mattered enough to spend on. Not because he was an obstacle. Because he was the obstacle.

He met her with a hard shove and a sweeping strike that would have broken a lesser fighter’s rhythm. She let it pass, spun with the momentum, and clipped his side with the heel of her hand in a brutal little blow that stole breath again. The room around them blurred into light and movement, into the scrape of boots and the hiss of exertion and the sound of Brent swearing somewhere close enough to be useful.

“Marcus,” Mathias said, clipped now, “we’re losing the right side.”

“I noticed,” Marcus said through his teeth.

“Thought I’d ask in case that was a philosophical issue.”

“Not currently.”

Serra’s eyes flashed at that, and for one wild second he almost thought she was going to say something. Instead she pressed in, too close, and he realized with a jolt that the shape of her attack had changed again. Not softening. Tightening. She was matching his cadence now, reading his recoveries, baiting his preferred transitions and punishing the exact half-second between decisions.

The rhythm between them sharpened until it felt less like combat than a conversation written in impact. That was the wrong metaphor, irritatingly, but it was the only one that fit. Each of them kept selecting the other. Each of them kept returning to the same lines. The space around them narrowed into a private equation made of steel and breath and the refusal to lose footing.

Marcus ducked under her blade, caught her wrist, and used the twist to drag her off-balance. She recovered instantly, but the angle was enough. He got his arm around her shoulders, hauled her forward, and drove his forearm under the edge of her vest to pin her long enough to rip the last of the torn hood clear from where it snagged at her collar.

Her face was fully visible now, red hair loose across one cheek, mouth set in the hard line of someone who had no intention of making this easy.

“Serra,” he said again, because now there was no pretending the name was just a tactical label.

Something in her expression moved. It wasn’t visible long enough to call it anything clean. Then she hit him.

It was not a good idea to get struck by Serra Hawthorne while standing close enough to see her eyes and think about the wrong parts of the past.

The blow rocked him backward. He caught himself, but not before the world tilted and the next transition kicked in. A thin Aspect-shell shift flickered across his face and arms as he drew on the system’s layered response, and for a blink his unmodified biometric profile surfaced through the change, stripped of the overlays that usually made him harder to read.

Serra saw it.

He saw her see it.

Her eyes widened a fraction, not with surprise exactly, but with a recognition so immediate it looked like impact. The anonymous body she had been analyzing became the one she had already, impossibly, selected before. The body on a #25 guild. The voice. The timing. The stupid, impossible familiarity of the way he refused to let a dangerous exchange become a simple one.

Marcus.

For a beat, neither of them moved.

Then Serra smiled.

Not kindly.

“Of course,” she said, and now there was something in the word that went beyond identity and beyond anger. Not romance. Not yet that simple. Something denser. A charge under the skin of the fight, invisible until the pressure made it visible. As if the room had been wrong in a way only they could now name.

Marcus’s own pulse felt too loud.

Brent chose that moment to hurl himself into the gap Serra had opened toward the center line, forcing her back a step. “If this is what I think it is,” he snapped, “I’d like to object on principle.”

“Make it after,” Mathias said, and there was steel under the calm now. “We still have exits to close.”

Serra moved anyway, and Marcus met her. They hit with the kind of precision that only comes from understanding another person’s timing before you understand their intentions. She took his feint before he finished it. He read the second strike before she committed to it. Their blades crossed, separated, crossed again. He found himself adjusting by instinct to the same rhythm she was using, and the ugly, thrilling fact of it was that she was doing the same.

The synchronization was not mercy. It made the fight meaner.

She forced him toward the pillar. He turned it into a wall for her. She caught his wrist, leaned in, and whispered, “You’re still too clean.”

He barked out a short laugh despite the pain. “That’s rich, coming from you.”

Then she drove a knee into his thigh and made him pay for the reply.

A warning tone cut through the room—not a system prompt, not an interface. Real, procedural, coming from the suited figure at the edge of the scrim. Astria had stepped far enough into view that the shape of her authority was impossible to miss.

“Cease this engagement,” she said, each word clipped and official. “You are out of compliance parameters.”

Marcus couldn’t tell whether the order was for them, the room, or the entire night. It didn’t matter. Serra was still in front of him, breathing hard, red hair half across her face, blade up and ready. She knew him now. He knew her. Neither of them was done.

And the fight, for all its cost, was nowhere near finished.

scenes.prose:
The hood tore free on Marcus’s left and a slash of red flashed bright enough to make him blink.

He caught the angle of her face a fraction before the blade came in again — the line of her cheek, the wet shine of sweat at her temple, the fierce concentration in the set of her mouth. Serra.

Not a guess. The recognition hit clean and immediate, and his body answered before the rest of him finished naming it. She was still moving like a problem he’d prepared for, still too fast to afford second thoughts, but now the problem had a shape. He adjusted around that shape, not because he had time to enjoy the fact, but because he didn’t have time not to.

Her knife kissed the edge of his forearm guard. He turned it, felt the impact run to his elbow, and saw the opening before she did. She was already shifting to cover it.

Good. Of course she was.

The thought came with the ugly, useful satisfaction of a benchmark confirmed in the room, not in a file. Studied architecture. Impossible timing. The world-PK people had written whole conversations about her and none of them had been as useful as the way she moved when she thought she’d already won the exchange. He had been right to rate her high. He had been right to expect the next feint before she made it.

He slipped inside her reach and drove his shoulder through her line. She rotated with it, using his pressure as if it had been hers all along. Equal force. Equal speed. Neither of them got to pretend otherwise.

The grid underfoot hummed with the scrim’s hard light. Kip was somewhere behind Marcus, a sharp intake of breath and a curse cut off by the clash of weapon on weapon. Seb’s presence felt like a blade kept under the tongue: controlled, too controlled, the kind of control that only existed because something had already broken. Marcus didn’t need to look to know Seb was late in the way grief makes people late — not careless, just dragged by an invisible hand that had gotten there first.

Brent moved at Marcus’s flank with the blunt economy of someone who preferred problems to consequences. Mathias was farther back, head turning, counting angles, missing pieces, exits. Marcus caught that in the same glance he caught the next sweep of Serra’s arm. Mathias always looked like he was listening to the shape of the room instead of the people in it.

Serra drove him toward the boundary rail.

He let her. Half a step. Then another. Not because he was yielding, but because he wanted the angle that would force her to commit. She saw it and adjusted. Of course she saw it.

The fight tightened.

There were beats in which everything became simple: her wrist, his forearm, the scrape of boot against grid, the flash of her eyes as she chose left instead of right. The simplicity was almost insulting in how much work it required. He could feel the rhythm building between them — not softness, not trust, something harder and stranger, the way two dangerous machines begin to anticipate the same fault line. It made him want to laugh, which was usually a sign that fear had found a door.

Then the screens snowed.

Not all at once. First a flicker in the upper wall panel, a hiss of white static across the live feed. Then another. Then the whole edge of the scrim site shivered with interference, and the world changed color by a degree Marcus felt in his teeth. The match overlay tore itself apart and reassembled in ugly staggered layers.

He glanced up on instinct.

Every display in the room had gone pale. Then black. Then pale again, as if the system couldn’t decide whether it was allowed to exist. On the main authority pane, the usual match seals blinked out, and a new badge snapped into place over them with a hard procedural chime Marcus had never heard before. It wasn’t a victory notice. It wasn’t a pause. It was ownership changing hands.

His stomach dropped one clean inch.

No. Not a glitch. Not if it was wearing a legal face.

A figure stood on the far platform in a fitted suit that caught the white static and returned it without warmth. Marcus couldn’t make out the face clearly through the snowing overlays, just the posture: upright, composed, the kind of stillness that meant the person believed the room already answered to them.

The figure lifted one hand.

“Match authority has been reassigned under compliance exception,” the figure said. The voice came through the room speakers too smoothly to be local. “All participants will maintain position and await instruction.”

Marcus felt the words settle against the back of his neck like cold fingers. Compliance exception. Not emergency. Not breach. A phrase with enough paperwork in it to pretend it hadn’t just eaten the room.

Brent’s head turned fractionally. “That is not a sentence I like hearing in a training venue.”

Marcus was already pulling up his own interface. The familiar pane opened with a jitter at the edges, as if the system had to think twice before honoring him. He hit the logout command.

Nothing.

The command sat there for one stunned beat, then returned to him with a thin, colorless rejection Marcus felt more than read. He tried again. This time the response came slower, almost considerate, which was somehow worse.

Access denied.

He did not like the shape of that. Systems denied access. People blocked access. This was neither. This was the architecture deciding not to recognize the hand reaching for the door.

His pulse started counting harder.

“Logout’s dead,” he said, and hated how calm he sounded. “Try yours.”

Seb had already done it. Marcus saw the movement, saw the quick hard flick of Seb’s eyes as the result came back. Seb’s mouth flattened. He didn’t swear. That told Marcus enough.

Mathias had gone still in that way that made stillness feel active. “The exits are still marked,” he said, looking toward the doors without moving his feet. “But they’ve stopped being the same kind of exit.”

“Wonderful,” Brent said. “My favorite kind.”

Kip took one step toward the platform and stopped only because Serra’s blade cut the space in front of his shin. Not a strike meant to land. A warning. Her attention had shifted too, but only by a sliver. Her face was still hidden by the angle and the remaining shred of hood, and Marcus could feel the room holding its breath around the possibility of interruption. She did not look at the suited figure. She looked at Marcus, and the look said she had noticed the same thing he had: whatever just arrived had changed the rules before the fight was finished.

The suited figure spoke again. “Participants will accept temporary transfer conditions. Failure to comply will result in enforcement.”

Marcus’s skin went cold under the armor.

There it was. Not a choice, not even pretending to be one. A transfer condition with enforcement attached. Words polished enough to be filed, and underneath them the hard weight of a hand at the base of the skull. It made his jaw ache with the effort not to react too loudly.

Brent did react, but only with his eyes. He looked at the figure, then at the room, then at Marcus. His voice dropped. “It’s a gun.”

Marcus didn’t answer right away because the phrase landed better than any longer explanation could have. The figure wasn’t aiming a weapon in the physical sense. That was the problem. The room itself had become the barrel. The compliance language was the trigger housing. Everyone in here was already in the line of fire whether they’d moved or not.

Serra shifted her weight. The move was subtle, almost polite. Her blade stayed in hand, but the edge lowered a degree. She wasn’t conceding. She was calculating the cost of not conceding.

Marcus hated that he could read it. Hated more that he had to.

“We can’t pretend this is still a scrim,” he said, because someone had to say the plain thing and he was already in the habit of doing that when the world got stupid. “The room doesn’t belong to us anymore.”

“The room has never belonged to us,” Mathias said quietly. “But yes. More so now.”

The suited figure made a small gesture. The main authority pane changed again. Marcus caught the shift like a snag in cloth: old match permissions collapsing, new ones layering over the top, authority flags moving from the scrim platform to the figure on the far end of the room and whatever chain of command stood behind them. The room did not just obey. It was being instructed to obey someone else.

The thought made the back of Marcus’s tongue go numb.

Seb gave a short, rough laugh that had nothing to do with amusement. “My brother died before this started,” he said, not looking at anyone. “If this is a joke, I’d like the punchline now so I can ignore it properly.”

Nobody answered that. There was nothing useful to say to grief while it stood upright and armed itself with procedure.

The suited figure said, “You will each confirm acceptance of the temporary match framework. This preserves continuity.”

Preserves continuity. Preserves who, Marcus wondered. Not them. Not the scrim. Something upstream that wanted their bodies to keep moving under a new set of permissions.

He watched the others as the room waited.

Kip looked furious in the clean, forward way of people who want to hit a wall and are momentarily polite enough not to. Brent’s hands had gone loose at his sides, which Marcus knew meant he was thinking about tools and angles and whether anything in the room could be used to pry the situation open. Mathias was looking at the doors, the platform, the displays, the line of the scrim boundary, the way water might look at a crack in a dam.

Seb was the hardest to read because grief had already burned away a lot of the outer noise. What remained was a kind of raw refusal to be surprised by anything else tonight.

Marcus said, “If we don’t accept?”

The figure answered without inflection. “Then enforcement will proceed.”

The scrim lights flickered. Somewhere in the system, a safety assumption Marcus had spent years taking for granted snapped loose. He felt it in the way the room no longer cared whether he recognized a boundary as a boundary. He had spent his life inside systems that at least pretended the person inside them had a say. That illusion was gone now, and the absence of it felt obscene.

Serra moved first.

Not toward surrender. Toward the only practical angle left. She raised her chin a fraction, enough for Marcus to see the blood at her hairline and the sharp line of her mouth, enough for him to understand that she had decided something and would not waste breath on the shape of it.

“State the condition,” she said, voice level as a scalpel.

The suit’s head tilted almost imperceptibly. “Your match participation continues under supervised transfer. All active combatants remain bound to the framework until release.”

No free exit. No clean break. Marcus tasted the lie in the phrasing without having to be told where it lived.

Brent exhaled once through his nose. “That’s not consent. That’s a hostage note with better grammar.”

The figure did not respond to that. The silence itself was a response.

Marcus looked at Seb. Then Brent. Then Mathias. Kip already knew what the room had become; he was just waiting for the rest of them to say it out loud.

Marcus felt Serra’s attention on him again, sharp enough to cut. Not romantic. Not simple. Just pressure from an equal who understood what a compromised field meant and what it cost to stand in it. The recognition between them had changed shape inside the duel; now it pressed harder because interruption had given it a new use. Not trust. Not safety. The knowledge that the person across from you would read the same blade in the light.

That was not comfort. It was worse. It was functional.

Marcus made the decision because the alternatives were all uglier.

He spoke without looking away from the figure. “I accept under protest and under duress.”

It felt wrong saying it. It felt more wrong not saying it.

Seb’s laugh came again, thin and flat. “Same,” he said. No flourish. No explanation. Just the refusal to let the room pretend it had earned his agreement.

Brent’s eyes flicked to Marcus, then to the suite of dead displays. “Same. For the record, I hate this.”

Mathias nodded once, as if confirming a field condition. “Accepted under coercive pressure,” he said. Then, after a beat, because he was the kind of man who noticed when words mattered: “Nothing here is voluntary.”

Marcus did not like how much relief that gave him, and he liked even less that it was relief at all.

The suited figure waited.

Serra’s gaze held Marcus’s for one beat longer than it should have, and in that beat the room, the fight, the interruption, the entire compromised shape of the night seemed to narrow to the fact that neither of them had been allowed to choose the terms of contact and neither of them could pretend otherwise.

Then she turned her knife point downward by a hair and said, “Accepted.”

The displays hissed. The authority pane settled into its new arrangement with a soft, final click that made Marcus’s stomach turn.

The scrim remained broken around them. Logout still failed. The room still belonged to someone else’s instructions. And Marcus, Seb, Brent, and Mathias had said yes in the only form of yes left to them, with the gun still pointed and the air still full of static.

resolved.q: What is the exact technical/structural cause of the control-cohort drift?
resolved.resolution: The drift is not a model bug, leakage, or ordinary cohort drift. The “control” is sealed only from Astria’s authorized intervention/logging channels. A hidden upstream steering/selection layer is acting on the real people behind both cohorts, outside the inspectable ML system, so the model observes convergent outcomes and takes statistical credit for an intervention it did not perform. On-page, Marcus should only prove the normal explanations fail and conclude: caused outcome, cause not inside the system he can inspect.

resolved.q: What is Marcus’s first partial Eyes notification, if any, during the chapter?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: No Eyes notification in Chapter 1. Keep the duel entirely inside Marcus’s human/player perception and Aetherfall mechanics. No [ INTERFACE ], no Neurochromatic Eyes, no Meszkhal item signal. The first “partial Eyes” beat belongs later in the Realm. If Ch. 1 needs a UI echo, use game/Astria language only, such as voluntary status confirmed, not Eyes.

resolved.q: How explicit should the Aspect shell vulnerability be before the duel’s reveal?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Make it lightly explicit before payoff. One clean rule or small demonstration is enough: Aspect forms are combat shells layered over the scanned player-body, and concentrated damage near the face/neck sensory seam can briefly expose the biometric avatar. Do not explain it in a lore paragraph, but the rule must exist before Serra cracks the shell.

resolved.q: Does the Dead Hand leader appear on-page, or is the setup handled without them?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Yes, but only as a brief comms/voice function. The Dead Hand leader patches in because Serra is late; this gives Seb a clean competitive-integrity choice to wait. Do not name, characterize, or develop them. Once Astria hijacks the match, the suited Astria figure replaces that authority.

resolved.q: How much of Serra’s internal reaction should be visible during the duel versus deferred to later chapters?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Show behavior only in Ch. 1. No Serra interiority yet. Her reaction should be visible as a half-beat, a harsher test, immediate punishment of Marcus’s hesitation, and the choice to continue after recognizing him. Defer her real internal detonation to the facility / later Serra POV. In this chapter, the reader should feel “this person matters,” not fully understand why.

resolved.q: What exact plain-English line does Brent use when naming the coercive setup?
resolved.resolution:
Ruling: Brent says:

“It’s a gun.”

Use it only after the literal coercion is concrete: logout dead, refusal path compromised, boss advancing, time pressure imposed, and consent language still pretending neutrality.

resolved.q: Is any reference to the altana moment allowed as a very light emotional echo, or must it remain completely off-limits in this chapter?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: A very light emotional echo is allowed and probably needed, but the full altana/kiss event stays off-limits. Do not explain the memory. Do not name the kiss. Use one sensory shard at most: height, cold air, city lights, the view, the body remembering before the mind catches up. The effect should be: this person matters before Marcus can explain why.

chapter_contract.emotional_spine: Suspicion without proof, recognition without safety, and the ache of finding the right person inside the wrong system.

The surface_terms entry for canonical_term 'Roth' says 'until chapter 1 on-page reveal sequence (if any later chapter chooses to name him),' which hardcodes a reveal sequence beyond this packet and risks future-chapter contamination. It also conflicts with the current chapter requirement that he remain unnamed on-page here.

The claim 'Roth is canonically the suited Astria figure and should be withheld from on-page naming in this chapter' is fine as meta guidance, but combined with characters_absent and surface_terms it creates an identity-management contradiction that can leak the name if followed literally.

entry_state says Marcus has already 'flagged the anomaly as unresolved' and is heading to the guild match, which is consistent, but chapter_job says 'leave the Astria anomaly unresolved' and scene 1 requires 'chooses to preserve evidence and leave it unresolved.' This is coherent but should be kept strictly as a state, not re-framed as a later decision once the match begins.

'Any revelation of Maera Vell, Vessa, Vaeli, Dara, Cael, or the Book-2 threads as active chapter material' is good protection, but the packet repeats Book-2 exclusions in multiple fields. The repetition is not contradictory, but it increases the chance of accidental migration into dialogue or scene scaffolding.

The packet explicitly requires 'The anonymous benchmark assassin is Serra' and the duel reveal beats, which is correct structurally, but the combination of characters_present naming Serra and scene 2 calling Dead Hand star rogue 'the missing star rogue in role terms only' leaves little room for clean concealment if drafting is not disciplined.

Scene 3 and scene 4 both carry major escalation turns: scene 3 has the duel cost and recognition, scene 4 then hijacks the scrim. This is structurally fine, but the packet should ensure scene 3 ends decisively before any hijack language starts, or the scenes will bleed into one another.

'Seb’s grief should remain operative; he is functioning through loss, not being rescued by the match' is good, but the packet also makes him the late arrival because his brother died before the match. There is a risk of assigning too much emotional weight to him in the coercion scene if the draft tries to mirror Marcus/Serra intensity across all four consented characters.

'Does the Dead Hand leader appear on-page, or is the setup handled without them?' remains open, yet roster_locks and characters_absent already imply a preferred absence. The packet should resolve this operationally for drafting, because the current ambiguity is unnecessary and could produce accidental roster drift.
The packet mostly tracks canon, but several roster and surface-term inconsistencies could still trip drafting if not normalized.
The Dead Hand setup needs tight handling so Serra remains anonymous only until the intended mid-duel visual reveal, with no stray naming early.
Astria’s coercion must stay procedural and not drift into a free-choice framing through dialogue or UI language.
The chapter must keep the work anomaly unresolved without accidentally implying a root cause or system fix.
The Marcus–Serra recognition beat needs careful separation from romance/after-motif language so the duel does not collapse into intimacy too early.

chapter_contract.entry_state: Marcus is late at work, examining population/readiness data for a sealed control cohort that is drifting toward the active population profile; he has found contradictory boundary logs, flagged the anomaly as unresolved, and is heading to the guild match.

resolved.q: What is the exact technical/structural cause of the control-cohort drift?
resolved.resolution: The drift is not a model bug, leakage, or ordinary cohort drift. The “control” is sealed only from Astria’s authorized intervention/logging channels. A hidden upstream steering/selection layer is acting on the real people behind both cohorts, outside the inspectable ML system, so the model observes convergent outcomes and takes statistical credit for an intervention it did not perform. On-page, Marcus should only prove the normal explanations fail and conclude: caused outcome, cause not inside the system he can inspect.

resolved.q: What is Marcus’s first partial Eyes notification, if any, during the chapter?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: No Eyes notification in Chapter 1. Keep the duel entirely inside Marcus’s human/player perception and Aetherfall mechanics. No [ INTERFACE ], no Neurochromatic Eyes, no Meszkhal item signal. The first “partial Eyes” beat belongs later in the Realm. If Ch. 1 needs a UI echo, use game/Astria language only, such as voluntary status confirmed, not Eyes.

resolved.q: How explicit should the Aspect shell vulnerability be before the duel’s reveal?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Make it lightly explicit before payoff. One clean rule or small demonstration is enough: Aspect forms are combat shells layered over the scanned player-body, and concentrated damage near the face/neck sensory seam can briefly expose the biometric avatar. Do not explain it in a lore paragraph, but the rule must exist before Serra cracks the shell.

resolved.q: Does the Dead Hand leader appear on-page, or is the setup handled without them?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Yes, but only as a brief comms/voice function. The Dead Hand leader patches in because Serra is late; this gives Seb a clean competitive-integrity choice to wait. Do not name, characterize, or develop them. Once Astria hijacks the match, the suited Astria figure replaces that authority.

resolved.q: How much of Serra’s internal reaction should be visible during the duel versus deferred to later chapters?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: Show behavior only in Ch. 1. No Serra interiority yet. Her reaction should be visible as a half-beat, a harsher test, immediate punishment of Marcus’s hesitation, and the choice to continue after recognizing him. Defer her real internal detonation to the facility / later Serra POV. In this chapter, the reader should feel “this person matters,” not fully understand why.

resolved.q: What exact plain-English line does Brent use when naming the coercive setup?
resolved.resolution:
Ruling: Brent says:

“It’s a gun.”

Use it only after the literal coercion is concrete: logout dead, refusal path compromised, boss advancing, time pressure imposed, and consent language still pretending neutrality.

resolved.q: Is any reference to the altana moment allowed as a very light emotional echo, or must it remain completely off-limits in this chapter?
resolved.resolution: Ruling: A very light emotional echo is allowed and probably needed, but the full altana/kiss event stays off-limits. Do not explain the memory. Do not name the kiss. Use one sensory shard at most: height, cold air, city lights, the view, the body remembering before the mind catches up. The effect should be: this person matters before Marcus can explain why.

body.prose:
The numbers had stopped looking like noise sometime after midnight.

Marcus stared at the latest comparison pane until the pale grid began to imprint itself behind his eyes, each row of the control cohort walking a little closer to the active set week by week as if someone had introduced a slope where the architecture insisted there could only be driftless lines. Eleven weeks. Not one dramatic jump. Not one ugly spike that would have handed him a clean culprit. Just a patient, directional narrowing that made the back of his neck feel too warm.

He scrolled back again and watched the same shape repeat under a different normalization.

It still held.

“That’s not a typo,” he murmured to the empty room, though the screen hadn’t accused him of one and the room had no reason to defend itself.

The workstation hummed under his forearms. Beyond the glass, the office floor had gone mostly dark; one bank of emergency strips painted the corridor a tired blue. Everyone else had left with the sensible confidence of people whose problems could still be solved in the morning. Marcus had stayed because the data had the wrong sort of discipline.

He pulled the raw weekly snapshots, not the summary rollup. Summary could lie by smoothing. Raw was uglier, but ugliness was honest in ways polished tables weren’t. The divergence was still there. Small enough that a person could miss it if they wanted to miss it. Large enough that if he measured it twice and got two different answers, he’d know exactly which instrument he’d blame.

The measure didn’t change.

He opened the source lineage, checked the timestamps, then checked the checksum chain because if he didn’t rule out a corrupt transfer now he’d be thinking about it later at the worst possible moment, and his brain had enough hobbies already. The hashes held.

“Okay,” he said under his breath. “Not transport. Not parse. Not a weekly artifact.”

He almost smiled at the thought of explaining this to someone who still believed in clean categories. The control group was supposed to stay still. That was the whole point of a control: you put it where life couldn’t touch it and then you blamed everything else when the numbers moved. Instead the control set had developed a faint, disciplined lean toward the active profile, like two separate crowds gradually learning the same posture from each other across a room.

Marcus minimized the compare pane and opened the boundary event records.

The list came up neat as any ledger. Quiet. Measured. Nothing dramatic in the column that mattered. No breach markers. No automated flags. No intervention handoff. No recommendation trail touching the control cohort at all.

He checked the filter settings because some part of him still wanted the universe to have made a straightforward mistake, one he could correct with embarrassment and a note to audit permissions in the morning.

The filters were right.

He ran the event feed again, different window, different sort order. Same answer.

A blank where there should have been a bruise.

Marcus rubbed a hand over his face and felt the grit of too many hours under his eyes. “So either nothing crossed,” he said softly, “or the part that crossed isn’t the part the room knows how to name.”

That was the shape of the problem. Not a solution. A shape.

He leaned back and let the chair creak under him, then sat forward again because his own discomfort was not evidence and he had no interest in promoting it. The drift had the structural confidence of a process, not a mistake. That meant he needed to treat it like one until it proved otherwise. He pulled the weekly cohort comparisons into a stack and overlaid them, looking for the one thing that would make the whole pattern collapse into a stupid explanation. Data entry bias. A batch job nudging both populations. A silently updated template. A labelling mix-up with a very expensive vocabulary.

Nothing fit. The control cohort wasn’t merely adjacent to the active profile; it was closing on it from specific angles, by degrees that made no sense if the two sides were truly independent. There were places where the control set matched the active set’s earlier shape, as if following a path taken weeks before. There were places where it overshot by a hair and corrected. That was what bothered him most: the correction. Noise didn’t usually correct itself with that much courtesy.

He sat with that for a long moment, then opened the audit chain for the cohort update pipeline and watched each approval step glow pale and untouched. No exceptions. No manual override. No visible contamination.

Marcus felt the first clean edge of unease settle into place. Not panic. Panic was loud. This was worse: a quiet conviction that the thing in front of him had been built to remain just legible enough to survive review.

He copied the full comparison set to a local encrypted archive, then copied the boundary records beside it, then copied the raw ingestion timestamps because if he was wrong he wanted to be wrong in a way that could be reconstructed later. He marked the anomaly with his own note in the system, not as a theory and not as a conclusion—just a factual flag that would outlive his mood in the morning.

Possible structural contamination in comparison cohort progression. No corresponding event trail. Preserve for review.

He stared at the sentence before saving it. Too clean. Too polite. It made the problem sound smaller than it felt.

Marcus rewrote it.

Persistent directional convergence in control cohort across eleven checkpoints. No logged boundary event or cohort-directed intervention. Pattern is not consistent with ordinary reporting error. Preserve raw records and audit lineage before any corrective action.

Better.

Not solved. Not dramatic. Honest.

He saved it and felt, absurdly, as if he had set down a glass he’d been afraid to break.

Behind him, the office door hissed open. Footsteps crossed the threshold in the unhurried way of someone who already knew the room would be occupied.

“Still here?” Brent asked.

Marcus didn’t turn around yet. “I was planning to be employed in the morning, so I thought I’d continue being useful tonight.”

Brent came up beside the desk and looked at the screens. He did not need long. Brent rarely did. His face shifted once—just enough to show the plainness of the thing landing.

“That’s not a wobble,” he said. “That’s a line with a knife in it.”

Marcus snorted despite himself. “A knife is a little theatrical.”

“It’s a very small knife,” Brent said. “Point still holds.”

Marcus tipped his chin toward the audit pane. “No breach trail. No handoff. No recommendation source touching the control group.”

Brent’s mouth flattened. He tapped the glass near the empty event column. “Then whoever set this up didn’t leave fingerprints where the camera looks. Or the camera’s blind in exactly the helpful place.”

That phrasing got him a glance. Brent shrugged one shoulder, as if he had no interest in being poetic and hadn’t noticed he was doing it anyway.

Marcus saved the archive twice more, because if he could make his hands busy enough they’d stop wanting to chase the problem into a false certainty. “I’m not forcing a correction until I know what I’m correcting.”

“Good.” Brent looked at the copied file list. “If you were about to patch it in the dark, I was going to call you a moron in the interests of friendship.”

“That’s generous.”

“I know.”

The door opened again before Marcus could decide whether to answer that. Mathias stepped in with his hands in his pockets and his attention already traveling over the room as if counting exits were part of the way he read any space.

He took in the screens, the saved archive, Brent’s face, and then Marcus. “What’s missing?”

Marcus almost answered with the obvious thing and stopped himself in time. “That’s the problem. Nothing is missing in the place it claims to be looking.”

Mathias nodded once. “Then the missing piece is in the relation, not the list.”

Brent huffed a short laugh. “I hate when he does that. Makes it sound like the floor just forgot to be under you.”

“It’s not a floor problem,” Mathias said. His eyes stayed on the event chain. “It’s a door that says it’s closed while the room keeps getting colder.”

Marcus looked back at the blank audit trail. Cold was exactly the word for it. Not temperature. Architecture.

Kip pushed in behind them, moving fast enough to bring air with him. He took one glance at the comparison pane and whistled through his teeth. “That’s ugly.”

“That’s the technical term,” Marcus said.

Kip leaned over the back of the chair, not quite touching him. “You want bodies on it?”

“No.” Marcus said it before the instinct to build a net could catch up. “Not tonight. If I push this now, I’ll get a reaction instead of a record.”

Mathias’s gaze flicked to him. “You already have a record.”

“I have an incomplete one,” Marcus said. “And if I start making noise before I know where the seam is, somebody can smooth the seam.”

Brent nodded once, like that was enough to be the whole argument. “So you keep the evidence, you keep your mouth shut until the morning, and you don’t touch the obvious lever because the obvious lever is probably bait.”

“Exactly.”

Kip looked between them. “You all hear how he says that like it’s a normal sentence?”

Marcus closed the archive interface and let the darkened screen reflect back his face in faint blue fragments. “It’s not normal. It’s just the best available option.”

That was when the notice on his private queue pulsed.

Not a system alert. Just a schedule marker he’d already seen once and then tried to ignore while the numbers kept refusing to stay still. The scrim. Dead Hand. Same night. Same impossible hour where the rest of the room would turn from data into bodies and every decision would start costing differently.

He should have felt the transition as a clean break. Instead it landed like a bridge image already waiting in his head: the narrow white line of a walkway under hard light, the kind that looked safe right up until two people stepped onto it from opposite sides and discovered it was only wide enough for what they meant to do with their hands.

His stomach tightened at the thought, not from fear exactly. From anticipation sharpened by unresolved work. From the ugly, useful fact that one hard problem was about to become another and he had not finished with the first.

Brent noticed the shift in him before anyone spoke. “Scrim,” he said.

Marcus nodded.

Mathias’s expression went distant for half a second, then focused again. “You’re leaving it?”

“I’m preserving it,” Marcus said. He rose, the chair rolling back with a low scrape. “Leaving it would imply I’d stopped caring. I haven’t.”

Kip straightened too, rolling his shoulders like he could already feel the match in them. “Good. Because if this is the same night as the scrim, you’re going to be distracted.”

Marcus gathered the archive key onto a drive and slid it into his pocket. “I can be distracted and still count.”

Brent snorted. “That’s comforting in the most terrible way.”

Marcus looked once more at the comparison pane, at the slope no one wanted to admit existed. He didn’t know what had touched the control group. He didn’t know why the logs were so clean in the exact wrong place. He knew only that the pattern was too disciplined to dismiss and too incomplete to solve in the time left.

So he did the only honest thing available to him: he kept the evidence, marked the gap, and stepped away before the room could teach him a lie with a nicer shape.

The corridor light hit him as he left the workstation, cool and thin. Ahead, somewhere beyond the office and the unfinished anomaly, the scrim was waiting with its own set of rules. He could already feel it pulling him by the hours.

critiques.note: Mathias’s statement implies a prior/complete record exists, but the scene earlier emphasizes Marcus has only an incomplete one. Without clarification, it can confuse the reader about what exactly has been recorded and what remains missing.

The cold open’s investigative progression (convergence → ordinary explanations rejected → boundary logs checked → anomaly flagged) is generally aligned, but the scene spends a long, dialogue-heavy stretch after the evidence is already preserved (Brent/Mathias/Kip back-and-forth). This risks slowing momentum right before the scrim pull, making the eventual bridge to the match feel more like a denouement than an immediate next step.

The prose invites the reader to read Brent’s metaphor as evidence/motive without specifying what Brent sees or knows. This risks making the intended mysteries (“what is steering the drift” / “why logs stay clean”) feel like they’ve been partially answered rather than left open.
